reasons: No. The bishop on c7 takes her, which is the whole idea.

bank.reason: The bishop on c7 is the only black piece attacking b8, and taking is the one thing it cannot do while staying on c7.

bank.prompt: Play it out: the queen offer, the capture, and the mate.
bank.reason: Qb8+ Bxb8 Rd8 is mate. f7, g7 and h7 are the king's own pawns and nothing covers d8 once the bishop has left c7.

bank.prompt: Two black bishops and a rook on a2, and only one of them is doing a job that matters. Find the move.
bank.reason: Qb8 is check and both Bxb8 and Bd8 empty c7, so Rd8 or Rxd8 is mate. The rook on a2 and the bishop on e4 never get a move.

bank.prompt: White takes the rook on a2 with the queen. Is the queen safe on a2?
reasons: No. The bishop on e4 takes her.
Yes. Nothing black attacks a2, so she keeps the rook.
No. The bishop on c7 takes her.
bank.reason: Nothing black attacks a2, so the rook is a free rook. It is still the wrong move: the bishop stays on c7 and the mate is gone.

bank.prompt: Qb8 gives up a queen for a bishop, and Qxa2 wins a whole rook for nothing. Why is the queen offer better?
options: Because the bishop on c7 is worth more than the rook on a2.
Because Qb8 buys d8, and d8 is mate, while the rook on a2 is only material.
Because Qxa2 would lose the queen to the bishop on e4.
bank.reason: Mate ends the game, so anything that buys mate outranks anything that wins material. The rook on a2 is genuinely free and genuinely irrelevant.

bank.prompt: The bishop on e5 is standing in front of your rook on e1. Offer it something on the far side of the board.
bank.reason: Rb8 is check, and the bishop on e5 is the only black piece attacking b8. Bxb8 opens the e-file and Re8 is mate; Qd8 blocks and Rxd8 is mate.

bank.prompt: Play it out: pull the bishop off the e-file, then mate down it.
bank.reason: Rb8+ Bxb8 Re8 is mate. The bishop was guarding b8 and blocking the e-file at once, and one check stopped it doing both.

bank.prompt: Your rook on d1 would mate on d8 if the file were clear. Clear it without taking anything.
bank.reason: Ra8 is check and the bishop on d5 is the only black piece attacking a8. Bxa8 opens the d-file; Qc8 blocks and Rxc8 mates instead.

bank.prompt: Tap the black piece that is standing between your rook on d1 and the mate on d8.
bank.reason: The bishop on d5 blocks the file, and nothing black covers d8 itself. It is also the only thing attacking a8, which is what makes Ra8 work.

bank.prompt: Play it out: the offer on a8, the capture, and the mate on d8.
bank.reason: Ra8+ Bxa8 Rd8 is mate. A rook was the price of one open file, and the file was worth it.

bank.prompt: Ra8 does not attack the bishop on d5 and does not defend anything. What does it do?
options: It threatens mate on a8 next move.
It attacks the pawn on a7, which is undefended.
It puts a rook where the bishop on d5 must take it, which is the one move that empties the d-file.
bank.reason: The bishop is the only black piece that attacks a8, so Ra8 with check forces it to leave d5. Nothing else on the board makes it move.

bank.prompt: The knight on c7 covers both a8 and e8. Make it choose, with check.
bank.reason: Ra8 is check and the knight has two answers, Nxa8 and Ne8. After Nxa8 the knight no longer covers e8 and Re8 is mate; after Ne8 either white rook takes on e8 with mate.

bank.prompt: White is about to play Ra8 with check. Tap every square the knight on c7 could legally go to in answer.
bank.reason: Nxa8 and Ne8 are Black's only two legal moves. The king cannot move and the queen on h5 cannot reach the eighth rank, so both of those squares lose.

bank.prompt: Play it out: the check on a8, the knight capture, and the mate.
bank.reason: Ra8+ Nxa8 Re8 is mate. The knight was covering e8 from c7 and it cannot cover it from a8.

bank.prompt: Nxf7 would hit the king and the queen at once, if the king were on h8 instead of g8. Put it there.
bank.reason: Rh8 is check and Kxh8 is the only legal answer. Nxf7 is then check and hits g5, so the queen goes next move.

bank.prompt: White plays the rook to h8 beside the black king. Is the rook safe there?
reasons: No. The queen on g5 takes it.
No. The king takes it, and that is what White wants.
Yes. The king is not allowed to capture on h8.
bank.reason: Kxh8 is Black's only legal move. Losing the rook is the price, and the king standing on h8 is what you bought.

bank.prompt: Tap the square your knight wants, from which it would give check and attack the queen at the same time.
bank.reason: From f7 a knight hits h8 and g5. It does not work yet, because from g8 the king defends f7; that is why the king has to be moved first.

bank.prompt: The knight on g5 can reach f7, and f7 hits h8 and d8. Arrange for the king to be on h8.
bank.reason: Rh8 is check with Kxh8 the only legal answer. Nxf7 then forks the king on h8 and the queen on d8.

bank.prompt: Play it out: the rook offer, the recapture, the fork, and the queen.
bank.reason: Rh8+ Kxh8 Nxf7+ and the king goes to g8 or h7. Either way Nxd8 follows: a rook for a queen.

bank.prompt: Rh8 gives up a rook and the king simply takes it. What has White gained?
options: The king is now on h8, which is a square the knight on f7 gives check from while also hitting d8.
The h-file is now open for the white king to walk up.
Black's king has lost the right to castle.
bank.reason: Nothing was removed from the board except White's own rook. The gain is the king's new square, chosen before the rook was given.

bank.prompt: Nd7 would hit f8 and b6, but f8 holds a rook, which would simply move away. Put the black king on f8 instead.
bank.reason: Rxf8 is check and Kxf8 is the only answer. The rook that could have run is gone and the king now stands on f8, so Nd7 forks king and queen.

bank.prompt: Play it out: trade on f8, then fork, then take the queen.
bank.reason: Rxf8+ Kxf8 Nd7+ and the king has four squares, none of which defends b6. Nxb6 wins the queen for a rook.

bank.prompt: The rook on b8 defends the knight on b6 and also covers f8. Make it pick one of the two.
bank.reason: axb6 takes the knight. Rxb6 wins it back and leaves f8, where the bishop on b4 holds a white rook, so Rf8 is mate. Anything else is a piece down.

bank.prompt: White plays the rook straight to f8, where the bishop on b4 defends it. Is the rook safe there?
reasons: No. The rook on b8 takes it along the eighth rank.
No. The king takes it, because the bishop on b4 does not reach f8.
Yes. The bishop on b4 defends f8, so nothing can take.
bank.reason: The king may not take, because the bishop on b4 covers f8, but Rxf8 is legal and it is Black's only move. The rook has to be dealt with first.

bank.prompt: Play it out: take the knight, let the rook win it back, and mate on f8.
bank.reason: axb6 Rxb6 Rf8 is mate. The bishop on b4 defends the rook on f8 and the king has nowhere else, so recapturing was the losing choice.

bank.prompt: Why does taking on b6 win, when axb6 Rxb6 is just a pawn for a knight?
options: Because the pawn on b6 will promote.
Because the rook on b6 is then attacked by the bishop on b4.
Because the rook on b8 was the only thing covering f8, and on b6 it no longer covers it.
bank.reason: One rook, two jobs. Black can keep the knight or keep f8, and f8 is mate, so the piece has to go.

bank.prompt: Same job, different helper: the knight on e6 covers f8. Give the rook on b8 two things to do at once.
bank.reason: axb6 attacks nothing new, it removes the knight. Rxb6 abandons f8, where the knight on e6 holds your rook, and Rf8 is mate.

bank.prompt: Tap the black piece that is doing two jobs at once.
bank.reason: The rook on b8 defends the knight on b6 down the file and covers f8 along the rank. It can keep one of them.

bank.prompt: Tap every white piece that attacks f8. That is why a rook can sit there and survive.
bank.reason: The rook on f1 down the file and the knight on e6. With f8 attacked twice and defended only by the king, a rook there cannot be taken.

bank.prompt: The knight on c6 has no legal move at all. Do not trade for it. Hit it again.
bank.reason: The knight is on the line from the bishop on b5 to the king on e8, so it cannot step aside. d5 attacks it a second time and costs nothing.

bank.prompt: White pushes the pawn to d5, right next to the black knight. Is the pawn safe on d5?
reasons: No. The knight on c6 takes it.
No. The pawn on b7 takes it.
Yes. Nothing black attacks d5, and the knight is not allowed to move at all.

bank.prompt: Why is d5 better than taking the knight with the bishop straight away?
options: Because Bxc6 lets bxc6 take back and gives up the very thing that froze the knight.
Because the pawn on d5 attacks the rook on h8 as well.
Because Bxc6 would be met by Kd7.

bank.prompt: One black piece is frozen. Bring the cheapest possible second attacker to it.

Yes. Nothing black attacks d5 at all.

bank.prompt: The knight on c6 is defended by the pawn on b7. Why does that not save it?
options: Because the pawn on b7 is itself attacked.
Because a pawn taking a knight is a good trade whatever defends it, and the knight is not allowed to run away.
Because the knight is not really defended; b7 does not cover c6.
bank.reason: Defenders answer the question of whether a trade is good. Against a pawn attacking a knight, one defender is not an answer, and the pin removes the third option of moving.
